neighbours.label: how living things grow and reproduce in natural-history prose: the verbs and linkers describing plants or microbes forming clumps, dividing, sprouting, dispersing seed, or being pruned while dormant; the same sentence frames about offices, meetings and machines stay low
fire: The willow spreads along the stream by sending up suckers and forms dense thickets.
Thrushes swallow the fruit and scatter the seeds far from the parent tree.
Cut the roses back in late winter when the plants are still dormant.
Yeast cells reproduce by budding and soon form a thick layer in the jar.
The fern forms new plants from runners that root wherever they touch the soil.
In spring, fresh shoots emerge from the base of last year's stems.
The algae divide rapidly into new cells when the water warms up.
Oaks are usually grown from acorns gathered in the autumn.
quiet: The committee meets in late winter when the office is still quiet.
Volunteers hand out the leaflets far from the town hall every Saturday.
The printer jams whenever the paper tray is filled too high.
The bakery opens early and soon has a long queue at the door.
The bus leaves from the station and stops wherever passengers ask.
In spring, the shop puts new bicycles in the front window.
The orchestra rehearses twice a week when the hall is free.
Our chairs are usually made from pine bought in the autumn.
